title: How do the Gumulgal say five, six and seven?
description: The Gumulgal people of Australia count in twos, with urapon for one and ukasar for two. The video builds their names for five and six by splitting each number into twos and a one, and finds the word for seven. Keeko's doubt is that five is three ukasars.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number name can be built by counting in groups of two, with a separate word for the one that is left. The Gumulgal had a single word, ras, for every number greater than six. Watch for students who write too many twos.

source: In the Gumulgal system, urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2. Build t
video_script.why: The child sees how number names can be built by counting in twos, and how the Gumulgal system stops at six.
video_script.substitution: Split each number into twos and a one, then say the word for each part.
video_script.anchor: the Gumulgal number names for one, two, three and four, each shown with pebbles in pairs
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says five is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar. Counting the twos gives two, four, six, so three ukasar make six, not five.
video_script.payoff_line: Five is two and two and one, six is three twos, and seven is ras

final_answer.value: 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and 7 is ras
final_answer.spoken: five is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, six is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and seven is ras

hold_back: 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and 7 is ras
never_show: the answer card before the last beat of the board solution
maths_rules: the Gumulgal called any number greater than 6 ras, so 7 is ras
video_script.design: One idea: split each number into twos and a one. The names for one to four stay on the stage; the names for five and six are built beside them.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the words urapon and ukasar appear, with one pebble under urapon and a pair of pebbles under ukasar; a question mark appears

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.words: the words urapon and ukasar appear, with one pebble and a pair of pebbles under them
marks.ask: a question mark appears beside the words

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the Gumulgal, a group of indigenous people in Australia.
<bookmark mark='words'/>In their system, urapon is one and ukasar is two.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What would their names for five and six be, and what would they say for seven?

beats.on_screen: the two words hold still and the question mark glows

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board and the question mark glows

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the names move to the stage; 3 = 2 + 1 is shown as a pair and a single pebble named ukasar-urapon; 4 = 2 + 2 is shown as two pairs named ukasar-ukasar

marks.three: a pair and a single pebble appear, named ukasar-urapon
marks.four: two pairs of pebbles appear, named ukasar-ukasar

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>The Gumulgal count in twos. Three is two and one, so its name is ukasar-urapon.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Four is two and two, so its name is ukasar-ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Given: urapon is 1; ukasar is 2; numbers are counted in twos

marks.given: the facts are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, urapon is one, ukasar is two, and numbers are counted in twos.

beats.on_screen: To find: the Gumulgal names for 5 and 6, and the word for 7

marks.find: the words To find are written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the names for five and six, and the word for seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: split 5 into twos and a one: 5 = 2 + 2 + 1

marks.m1: five pebbles split into two pairs and a single pebble, and 5 = 2 + 2 + 1 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, split five into twos and a one.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Five is two plus two plus one.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: each 2 is ukasar and the 1 is urapon, so 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon

marks.m2: each pair is labelled ukasar, the single pebble is labelled urapon, and the three labels join into one name

narration: <bookmark mark='s2'/>Step two, say the word for each part.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each two is ukasar, and the one is urapon. The name is ukasar-ukasar-urapon.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 6 = 2 + 2 + 2, three twos, so 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar

marks.m3: six pebbles split into three pairs, each pair labelled ukasar, and 6 = 2 + 2 + 2 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, do the same for six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Six is two plus two plus two. That is three twos, so the name is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: 7 is greater than 6, and the Gumulgal called any number greater than 6 ras, so 7 is ras

marks.m4: the line of names stops at 6, and 7 is placed after it under the word ras

narration: <bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, look at seven.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Seven is greater than six. The Gumulgal called any number greater than six ras.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and 7 is ras

marks.res: the three names glow one after another

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Five is two and two and one, six is three twos, and seven is ras.
<bookmark mark='res'/>In the Gumulgal system, five is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, six is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and seven is ras.

beats.on_screen: Keeko appears beside the board with a raised hand
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 5 as ukasar-ukasar-ukasar; three pairs of pebbles are counted as 2, 4, 6; the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows five as ukasar-ukasar-ukasar
marks.count: three pairs of pebbles are counted aloud as 2, 4, 6
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and the single urapon pebble returns

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks five is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Count the pebbles pair by pair, two, four and then six.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Three ukasar make six, which is one too many for five.
